author: jtraglia
content: First, I want to ack that someone could front-run your PQ data registration. An attacker/spammer could do this repeatedly, since you can register multiple times & then just register real PQ data later. It would be pretty annoying, since you'd have to either (1) wait until they change their PQ data or (2) try registering again with different PQ data.

author: jtraglia
content: Hmm adding the XMSS signature would take up ~2 GiB on the EL. On the bright side, we wouldn't store the signature in the state on the CL 😅

author: jtraglia
content: And we'd want to drop the limit from 1024 to 32, max ~80 KiB per payload. Per each of the two request types.

author: jtraglia
content: Dropping the uniqueness checks wouldn't be sufficient. When processing at the next fork, we could ignore duplicate keys/roots. But that wouldn't prevent an attacker from front-running you & just keeping the your PQ data. They'd be unable to perform duties, but maybe that don't care. I'd argue this is worse, because you might not notice they front-ran you.

author: jtraglia
content:
I see two solutions:
* (1) Accept that front-running is possible, but wouldn't be much of an issue in practice. You could pay a higher priority fee with new PQ data.
* (2) Add an XMSS signature to the request, accept higher storage on the EL, and reduced request limits.

author: potuz
content: The reason to go with the EL vs CL is that we have already tried to send arbitrary CL signed messages on Capella, and we all still have nightmares about it. On the CL side it requires to add a new topic to broadcast these messages, it requires to prevent DOS on this topic, it requires to rate limit peers, to write the validator client code to sign a new type of message, to update external signers, etc... on the EL, a la 8483 we do not need to do anything the EL takes care of spam prevention by gas charges and the CL only needs to add a trivial handler for the request. It is infinitely simpler. There is no need to check for proof of possesion because of the lack of algebraicity of the signature scheme

author: potuz
content:
ok, so this means that I have been trying to submit pre-registrations for months and this griever has frontrun me every time, I take several months until we do the P fork and then that fork comes in and all PQ data is consumed but mine cause I am not able to put my key because this guy keeps frontrunning my validator key. During that fork my validator keeps working and I continue attempting to deposit and this guy keeps spending gas to register my key and frontrun me and then we go into the second fork and I have not been able to register my key. Do I lose money? no my validator is withdrawn to my address. 

The attack is very very annoying, but it costs money to the attacker and it can't result on loss of funds. The "fix" for this particular attack seems to me that is not worth the trouble, it makes the pre-registration more complex for everyone across the pipeline:

- users need to pay much more, we could be talking potentially a lot of money for staking pools that will need to pay these txs themselves instead of the operator.  
- The tooling to generate the preregistration becomes more complex since you not only need to output the pubkey but you now also need to sign the message, something that again for pools would require the operator to generate both pubkeys and sign a message that could potentially require interaction with the tx (depending how the system is designed). 

Other than the above points I don't see any problem in requiring the proof of posession, but I think already the above is more than enough of a bad tradeoff

author: potuz
content: BTW, the frontrunning attack will also happen for actual PQ deposits unless we do the check for deposits as well, which I think we should not

author: tcoratger
content:
Yes, I agree with <@774033563732541451>. The situation you describe <@755590043632140352>—where you try to harass someone for months—is a case where you have a grudge against a specific individual and begin front-running them from the very start, leading to a back-and-forth struggle between the attacker and the target, potentially continuing right up until the final block.

However, there is another possibility: the attacker does absolutely nothing until the very last block, at which point they submit a registration transaction for every validator that hasn’t yet been registered! In this scenario, all those validators would be blocked and rendered unable to take any action because we are are the last block before cut-off.

So the tradeoff is:
- If you're quite late in the PQ-registration phase, you increase your risk of being front run (i.e. no "months" since there are days left or similar). you get ejected and might need to re-deposit to be a validator again.
- The PQ-registration should be assume it can fail and you need to re-generate a new PQ and re-try; compared with the proof option where you can know nobody can front run you. so fire and forget without checking things.
